Gopher rules: Place a checker next to one enemy checker and no friendly checkers. Last player to place a checker wins. Thanks to the BGA developer community for assisting me with this program, especially Sunil Patel. The checkers in Gopher are photos of backgammon checkers manufactured by Crisloid, in Rhode Island, USA. [Rating: 5/10] The early stages are so loose, I get impatient for the end game.  I wish there were barriers in the middle of the playing field or something else to push against early on.

[Rating: 5/10] I love abstract games with extremely simple rules and Mark Steere is a big name indeed in this field. Unfortunately, I couldn't understand this game. I mean, I understand the rules, of course, but I can't find a way to enjoy it. The first 3/4 of the game seem just an (almost random) preparation for the last turns where you try to look ahead some turns and not be the one to screw.

[Rating: 5/10] Not a bad abstract, but there's little room for creativity - the game is just getting an advantage in closing off possible paths. It's hard to dislike a no luck abstract because there is always depth of strategy, but none of the decisions in Gopher feel fun enough to want to come back to.

[Rating: 5/10] Visually interesting, looks like atoms forming a molecule.  But the liberties are hard to grasp.

[Rating: 5.5/10] A good introductory abstract game. Very easy to learn.  Place pieces following the placement rules until someone doesn't have a legal move.

[Rating: 6/10] On your turn, place a stone of your color adjacent to exactly one opponent stone and no others. Last to place a stone wins. There is strategy, but it's mostly just limiting your opponents options as you go. Not very satisfying. The board feels bigger than it needs to be, but it's still a short game.
